input:
This passage sets out the inventory policy that is proposed for a particular resin grade held in stock. Demand for this grade occurs at a mean rate of 1020 units per week, although there is appreciable variation around that mean, with a standard deviation of 287 units per week. When stock is replenished, the replenishment lead time is 7 weeks, which is a relatively long period during which demand must be met from the stock that is on hand.

Over a lead time of 7 weeks, the expected demand is 1020 x 7 = 7140 units. Because actual demand fluctuates, however, ordering only when stock falls to the expected lead-time demand would lead to stock being exhausted in roughly half of all replenishment cycles. A safety stock is therefore held in addition, and the safety stock that corresponds to a 95% cycle service level is 1253 units. Adding the two components together, the reorder point becomes 7140 + 1253 = 7766 units: when the stock position falls to 7766 units, a replenishment order is placed.

It should be noted that the policy rests on the assumptions that demand is normally distributed and that the demands in successive weeks are independent of one another. Seasonal peaks in demand are excluded from the analysis, and those figures should consequently be understood as applying to demand outside those peaks. A safety stock of 1253 units is, in summary, the quantity that the policy requires.
target:
Materials planning should hold a safety stock of 1253 units of the resin grade, with the reorder point set at 7766 units.

Demand for the grade averages 1020 units per week, with a standard deviation of 287 units per week, and replenishment has a lead time of 7 weeks. Average demand over the lead time is 1020 x 7 = 7140 units. The reorder point is that average plus the safety stock, 7140 + 1253 = 7766 units. The safety stock is the part of the policy that carries the service level: it is the buffer that holds the cycle service level at 95% against the week-to-week spread in demand during the 7 weeks in which an order is outstanding. The average component of the reorder point covers expected use; the safety stock covers the variation around it, and the two parts should not be merged when the policy is reviewed.

The reorder point is a trigger on the stock position, which counts stock on hand together with stock already on order. When the position falls to the reorder point, an order is placed, and the stock on hand at that moment has to carry demand until the order arrives. Setting the trigger on the position rather than on the shelf alone prevents a second order being placed while an earlier one is still outstanding, and it keeps the safety stock intact as a reserve against variation rather than as working stock.

The figures rest on two stated assumptions. Demand is treated as normal, and demand in one week is treated as independent of demand in the next. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand figures altogether. The policy is therefore a policy for ordinary demand: in a peak, the stock of 1253 units is consumed faster than the variation model supposes, and that service level is not delivered by this stock level under peak conditions.
